 Canmore tightens vacancy tax rules for 2027 after nearly $1M revenue shortfall
 The Town of Canmore is ending late declaration flexibility and mid-year vacancy tax adjustments in 2027 after falling nearly $1 million short of budgeted revenue this year 
 Jessica Lee 
 Oct 22, 2026 2:30 PM 
 Share by Email 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on X 
 Share on LinkedIn 
 Print 
 Share via Text Message 
 Canmore Civic Centre. RMO FILE PHOTO 
 CANMORE – The Town of Canmore is tightening rules around its vacancy tax in 2027, eliminating flexibility for property owners who miss declaration deadlines or change residency status after the municipality fell nearly $1 million short of its expected tax revenue this year.
 The changes follow provincial legislation that exempted qualifying Alberta residents from the higher tax rate but also required the Town to make mid-year reassessments and tax adjustments. Property owners will face a firm Dec. 31, 2026, declaration deadline, with no opportunities to submit additional information afterward.
 “Moving forward, no extensions will be given to property owners who don’t declare by the required deadline,” said Chelsey Gibbons, the Town’s manager of finance, in an update to council at its committee of the whole meeting Tuesday (Oct. 20).
 Properties sold to qualifying Alberta residents during the taxation year will also no longer be reassessed solely because of the change in ownership.
 Some councillors, however, questioned whether the stricter rules could unfairly penalize property owners whose circumstances change or who fail to submit their declarations on time for other reasons.
 “I am concerned about fairness, and I feel that being able to update a status in a system creates fairness,” said Coun. Tanya Foubert.
 The changes follow amendments by the provincial government to the Municipal Government Act (MGA) under Bill 28, which received royal assent in May and exempted qualifying Alberta residents from Canmore’s higher tax rate on non-primary residences.
 The vacancy tax, which rolled out this year to encourage full-time residency and generate revenue for housing initiatives, adds about 0.4 per cent of a property’s assessed value to regular municipal taxes for non-primary residences, or homes that are not occupied at least 183 days of the year. The Town had budgeted $4.4 million in revenue from the tax in 2026.
 The provincial legislation also introduced temporary provisions for 2026 requiring municipalities to recognize certain changes in eligibility during the tax year, including when properties were sold to Alberta residents or owners established their Alberta residency after the declaration deadline.
 Those provisions expire at the end of the year. 
 Gibbons said the temporary measures have resulted in repeated property reassessments and tax adjustments, creating significant administrative work for the Town and introduced “uncertainty into tax administration and revenue forecasting.”
 “For the 2026 tax year, under-collection was close to a million dollars, or roughly 23 per cent of the total [$4.4 million] budget set,” she told council.
 So far this year, the Town has processed 162 vacancy tax adjustments for property owners who failed to declare their residency status before the deadline but later established they were Alberta residents.
 Another 11 properties were reassessed after being sold to qualifying Alberta residents, and council has also granted tax relief to 18 property owners who missed last year’s declaration deadline despite their homes being occupied – as the Town considers – as a primary residence, including 11 who had a combined $51,194 in vacancy taxes cancelled for the year.
 Coun. Rob Murray questioned how the lost revenue would affect funding commitments already approved by council, including a planned $10 million contribution to the Banff YWCA-led Moustache Lands housing project over four years, starting in 2027. 
 Gibbons said administration has been managing expenses to offset the shortfall, but the reduced revenue could mean taking longer to achieve housing objectives.
 “As we’ll cover as part of the finance committee budget process this fall, we’ll likely need to look at longer timeframes to achieve the intended outcomes of the program, given these new revised revenue targets,” she said.
 Coun. Jen Marran questioned what, if any, options would be available to property owners who completed their declarations on time but experienced a change in circumstances during the year.
 “Any new information that comes forward after that point in time, especially once the tax notices have gone out, would only be considered for the following taxation year,” Gibbons noted.
 For properties changing hands, administration said buyers and sellers could negotiate how property taxes are divided through the statement of adjustments prepared as part of a real estate transaction.
 Coun. Wade Graham noted that this would give buyers an opportunity to account for the higher tax rate when negotiating a purchase.
 Foubert also questioned whether the Town could introduce a process similar to its supplementary property tax system, allowing changes to be captured at a single point later in the year rather than through continuous reassessments.
 Gibbons said that approach would still create revenue shortfalls because the Town’s tax rates and budget are established using an assessment base determined before the tax year.
 Foubert further questioned why council was not being asked to decide on the changes, particularly given her concerns about fairness for property owners.
 Sally Caudill, CAO with the Town, said the municipality’s adjusted approach is about complying with provincial legislation rather than introducing a new policy requiring council approval.
 “I don’t see this as a decision point for council. I see it as an MGA compliance issue,” she said.
 For Alberta residents who miss the declaration deadline and are charged the higher tax rate – as was the case with the 18 property owners granted relief by council this year – Marran questioned what recourse would be available to them. 
 Gibbons said property owners who fail to provide the required information to the assessor by the Dec. 31 deadline would lose the ability to challenge their assessment through the Assessment Review Board.
 They could still seek tax relief directly from council under a section of the MGA, however, as those 18 property owners did this year, although approval would remain at council’s discretion.
 Each of those owners had $500 retained from their tax refunds to cover administrative costs. Now, the Town plans to introduce a formal cost-recovery fee for such requests and develop a policy in 2027 clarifying which circumstances council would consider for relief.
 Mayor Sean Krausert said property ownership comes with responsibilities, including submitting required information on time.
 “If you fail to provide information, the regulations indicate that your property will be assessed based on the best information available, and that if you haven’t complied, you have to take responsibility for that,” he said.
 The Town is preparing an expanded communications campaign ahead of the declaration period leading up to the deadline, including mailed notices, utility bill inserts, weekly advertising, social media posts and newsletters.
 Adam Robertson, communications advisor with the Town, said the campaign would emphasize that property owners who do not complete their declarations will be subject to the higher tax rate. 
 “We’re going to advertise every week. We’re going to boost a bunch of social media posts. We’re going to do a whole bunch of direct e-newsletter in addition to the mail letters we use,” he said.
 “We’re taking everything we’ve done and kind of doubling it.”
